worksheet.title: The Missing Block
worksheet.subtitle: Add the block that's missing
worksheet.learning_goal: I can fix a program by adding a missing block.

parts.title: Not far enough!
parts.text: Sometimes a program is MISSING a block, so Bit falls short and never reaches the target. Run the code, see how far short it is, and add the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: Program 1 — target is 4
parts.note: Write the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: Run it — too short
parts.prompt: Run Program 1 from 1 (forward 2). What number does Bit land on? How many more does it need to reach 4?

parts.title: Add the missing block
parts.prompt: Write the block that gets Bit from where it stopped to 4. Run the fixed code — what number now?

parts.title: Program 2 — target is 1
parts.note: Write the missing block in the empty space.

parts.title: You try — add to fix
parts.prompt: Run Program 2 from 4 (back 1). It lands on 3, not 1. Write the missing block so Bit reaches 1. What block did you add, and where does Bit land?

parts.title: Big idea
parts.text: If a program falls short, it may be missing a block. Add the step that finishes the job so Bit lands right on the target.

parts.title: What this worksheet teaches
parts.text: Students fix a bug where the program falls SHORT of the target because a block is missing; they add the missing step and run again. Adding a step to fix the result is a kind of debugging. No coding experience needed.

parts.title: Before you start (no computer needed)
parts.text: No computer — paper and a pencil. You read each prompt aloud. Optional: tape a number line 0 to 5 on the floor and mark the target, so students can walk the buggy program and feel Bit miss.

parts.title: How to lead it (about 20 minutes)
text: 1. Show them (you do). Run a program that stops short of the target — it is missing a step.
2. Do one together. Exercise 1 — Program 1 stops on 3, one short of 4.
3. Let them try. Students write the missing block to reach the target (Ex 2), then fix Program 2 (Ex 3).

parts.title: Answer key (these are the verified correct answers)
text: Exercise 1 — Program 1: 1, forward 2 → 3. Bit is on 3, one short of 4.
Exercise 2 — add "forward 1": 1 → 3 → 4. Bit reaches the target, 4.
Exercise 3 — Program 2: 4, back 1 → 3. Add "back 2": 3 → 1. Bit reaches the target, 1. (Two "back 1" blocks also work.)

parts.title: If students get stuck — and ways to adjust
text: Watch for: changing a block instead of adding one. Here the fix is to put a step in.
Make it easier: count how far Bit still needs to go, then write a block for that distance.
Make it harder: ask for two different missing blocks that both reach the target.

parts.title: Ontario curriculum link (official wording)
text: C3.1 — solve problems and create computational representations of mathematical situations by writing and executing code, including code that involves sequential events.
In plain terms: students follow (or write) step-by-step instructions, in order, to get a result.
C3.2 — read and alter existing code, including code that involves sequential events, and describe how changes to the code affect the outcomes.
In plain terms: students read a program, change a block to fix it, and explain what the change did.

parts.title: You'll know it worked when
parts.text: The child adds the missing block so Bit reaches the target.
